parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem:
Nuclei X and Y are different isotopes of the same element.

Nucleus X is unstable and emits a $\beta^{+}$ particle to form nucleus Z.

By comparing the number of protons in each nucleus, state and explain whether the charge of nucleus X is less than, the same as or greater than the charge of:

markscheme_points.text: X has same number of protons as Y (and so) charge of X is the same as the charge of Y

hints: Hint 1: Think about what makes two nuclei isotopes of the same element - what nucleon number stays the same and what changes?
parts.proper_answer: The same as. X and Y are isotopes so have the same number of protons, and nuclear charge depends only on proton number.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Isotopes Really Means**
Think of the proton number $Z$ as the ID card for an element. Two nuclei can only be the same element if they have exactly the same $Z$. Isotopes differ only in neutron number $N$, so mass number $A$ is different.

Step 2: **Link Protons to Charge**
Each proton carries charge $+e$ and neutrons are neutral, so the total charge of a nucleus is $+Ze$. Since X and Y have the same $Z$, they have the same charge $+Ze$.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Recall what happens inside the nucleus in $\beta^+$ emission - which nucleon changes into which other nucleon?
Hint 2: If that nucleon change alters the proton number $Z$ by one, how does the total nuclear charge $+Ze$ of X compare with Z?
parts.proper_answer: Greater than. In $\beta^+$ decay a proton changes to a neutron, so X has one more proton than Z and therefore greater charge.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture $\beta^+$ Decay**
In $\beta^+$ decay a proton in the nucleus converts: $$p \rightarrow n + \beta^+ + \nu_e$$ So the parent nucleus loses one proton and gains one neutron. Proton number $Z$ decreases by 1, while nucleon number $A$ stays the same.

Step 2: **Compare X and Z**
X is the parent, Z is the daughter. That means $Z_X = Z_Z + 1$. Since nuclear charge is $+Ze$, more protons means more positive charge, so the charge of X is greater than the charge of Z.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem: Hadrons can be divided into two groups (classes), P and Q. Group P is baryons.
parts.text: State the name of group Q.
hints: Hint 1: Hadrons are particles that feel the strong force - remember there are only two families in this classification, and one is already given as baryons.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **The Two Hadron Families**
All hadrons interact via the strong nuclear force. You only need to remember two groups: baryons, such as protons and neutrons, and mesons, such as pions and kaons. So if group P is baryons, group Q must be mesons.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Describe, in general terms, the quark structure of hadrons that belong to group Q.
hints: Hint 1: Contrast with baryons, which are made of three quarks - what simpler quark combination makes the other hadron family?
parts.proper_answer: Consists of one quark and one antiquark.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Quark Make-up of Mesons**
Baryons are $qqq$ - three quarks. Mesons are the simpler combination: one quark paired with one antiquark, written as $q\bar{q}$. A common mix-up is to say two quarks, but you must include that one is antimatter - an antiquark.
